title: Strength standards are useless
summary: A structured thesis arguing that strength standards are arbitrary, serve no clear purpose, are wrongly used as size standards, and create toxic deadlines and psychological plateaus. He argues strength and size are correlated only within the individual, that rushing standards sabotages the newbie phase, and that the only relevant standard is one you set yourself.
claims: No strength standard is objective: they are either invented by YouTubers from their own experience and biases or averaged from mass anecdotal data
Different pages give different standards (one says a standard bench is 225 lb, another 315 lb), so there is no way to know whom to trust
Online strength databases do not filter their data: most entries come from novices, so averages skew the standards low; they use averages instead of medians
Databases cannot verify submissions: people lie about lifts out of ego and log improper lifts like half squats, further corrupting the numbers
Many YouTubers push standards they never met themselves, e.g. calling you a loser if you can't bench 3 plates within two years; standards are rooted in ego, not rigor
Lifting proficiency labels (beginner to elite) are defined solely by strength numbers; they would be useful only if based on work capacity, volume tolerance, frequency and recovery ability
Whether you can do an 'intermediate program' should not depend on a bench number; his programs expect experience and work capacity, not a strength threshold
If you want to know where you stand competitively, use competition standards for your strength sport, not YouTube strength standards

By Strength Level standards he is 'advanced' with a 485 lb deadlift at 210 lb bodyweight and a 330 lb front squat, yet national-level lifters at his weight pull at least 600 lb and records exceed 700-800 lb; light Chinese weightlifters beat his front squat
Average-based standards compare you to weaklings and lower your ambitions; do not use him as a strength authority, a natural powerlifter at his weight would pull seven plates
Most people actually use strength standards as size standards ('lift X and your legs will look like Y'), which is a childish argument
Linking a strength number to muscle size ignores leverages, past lifting experience and muscle memory, nervous system differences, training style and time spent lifting
A long-armed lifter benches less but works through a longer range of motion and may build a bigger chest than a short-armed lifter at the same strength
Someone who reaches a 2-plate overhead press in three years will not have the same shoulders as someone who reaches it in one, because tonnage, volume, intensity, frequency and recovery differ
Standards are one-size-fits-all: like forcing 100 people into a size 11.5 shoe, a universal standard ends up fitting no one
Standards are always round plate numbers (225, 315, 405) that exist only because of 45 lb plates; nothing in nature makes a 2-plate bench special
'A 3-plate bench gives a big chest' is trivially true because the bar is set so high, like telling someone to get a physics PhD to be good at math; a big chest can come with far less weight
Instead of chasing a 7-plate deadlift for big traps, a 5-plate deadlift plus shrugs would give similar results
Inverting the logic ('20-inch arms means a strong curl') shows how illogical size-from-strength standards are
Strength-gifted lifters with good leverages or nervous systems hit standards without the promised size and despair; many skinny people press 2 plates overhead with small shoulders
Less gifted lifters fail to reach the number in the promised timeline, blame themselves and give up on aesthetics
He reached a 3-plate bench after being told it would reveal all of life's answers and felt absolutely nothing: PR culture sells milestones that change nothing
People bulk to raise their bench because more mass helps pressing, abandoning their original goal of a bigger chest
The teenage 4-plate deadlift obsession leads to uncomfortably high-body-fat bulks, sloppy form and back injuries that sabotage lifting careers
Size and strength are correlated within the individual but not codependent; the arrow points both ways and you can trade one for the other
Clone example: one clone squats daily to rush a 3-plate squat (strength but little volume), the other squats 2-3 times a week plus other knee-flexion work; the weaker one may end up with bigger quads
Jonnie Candito has said he lost size while adding to his total, showing size and strength can move in opposite directions
After a squat injury near 3 plates he regressed to 2 plates; when he got back to 3 plates his legs were bigger than before at the same strength
Specializing in strength can sabotage the pursuit of size
Weight on the bar is far more gratifying than slow measurement changes, which explains the popularity of 5x5 and Starting Strength-style templates and why many people chasing size drift into strength
Newbie gains are poison for the brain: the rapid gratification makes people crash and quit when progress inevitably slows
Strength standards exist because YouTubers needed knee-jerk answers to unanswerable questions like 'when will I have a big chest'; honest answer is no one knows, put in the work
The stigma of being a 'noob' makes people rush the newbie phase: bad form, no technique, too much weight gained, and they never build a base
Most lifters who don't quit early quit on reaching 'intermediate', because they rushed to get there, expected magic and changed nothing
He defines an intermediate as someone who starts programming for themselves
Attaching deadlines to standards ('hit it in two years or you suck') adds shame, drives ego lifting, and the idea of wasting newbie gains is a false clock that biology doesn't follow
Standards create psychological plateaus at round numbers: he stalled at a 3-plate bench until someone loaded 325 lb and he pressed it easily
A record-breaking powerlifter said he only learned he was strong at his first meet because he had never compared himself to anyone or checked standards
Aiming for a number can be a valid goal, but pick it yourself rather than letting others set your limits
exercises: 4-plate obsession leads to ego lifting and back injury; 5 plates plus shrugs suffices for traps
pair with a moderate deadlift for trap size instead of chasing huge deadlift numbers
long arms mean more ROM, less weight, possibly more chest growth
2-plate OHP does not guarantee big shoulders
more volume builds quads better than daily low-volume squatting
